title: Mehtab Singh and Sukha Singh
hookLine: two Sikhs rode into Amritsar in disguise to end a desecration of the Harmandir in 1740

cards: Far to the south, in the dry country where hunted Sikhs had taken refuge, a traveler from Amritsar arrives with news nobody wants to hear.
The Harmandir, the house of the Guru at the center of the sacred pool, has been taken over by a local official.
Tradition says he is using it for drinking parties and dancing, inside the place where the Guru's hymns are sung. The listeners are silent. Then two men stand up.

teach.b: The official was named Massa Ranghar, and in the tradition he becomes a picture of contempt: someone who took a holy place and filled it with exactly what it was not for. Mehtab Singh and Sukha Singh decided to end it.
They could not march an army into Amritsar, so they used a disguise.
Tradition says they dressed as village headmen coming to pay revenue, and filled their bags with something that clinked like coins; some tellings say broken pieces of pottery, cut round.

They rode into Amritsar, tied their horses outside, and walked in carrying their bags as if they had come to pay what was owed. They were let through. Inside, they found Massa Ranghar at his entertainment.

teach.h: IN AND GONE BEFORE THE GUARDS KNEW.
teach.b: Tradition says they struck him down, and were back on their horses and gone before the guards understood what had happened. The story is told with fire, and it's worth saying what the tradition sees in it.
Not a love of violence. The Harmandir belongs to the Guru and to everyone who comes to it; its doors, Sikhs say, open in every direction. Using it for mockery was an attack on what it stands for.
The two riders were not after loot or power.

They rode in to give the place back to its purpose. A hard story, honestly told. But the image that stays is the two horses outside the gate, and two men who had every reason to stay safe in the desert, choosing not to.

how: Sikhs tell the story of Mehtab Singh and Sukha Singh as a defense of the Harmandir's sanctity, and it is often recalled in gurdwara talks about the Khalsa's hard century.

o: a Sikh who rode in to free the Harmandir
the official who held parties in the Harmandir
a village headman bringing revenue to pay

games.q: two riders, one purpose — tap the pairs.

s: Mehtab Singh and Sukha Singh came with a large army
they were two men, in disguise, with bags that clinked like coins.
the news reached them far from Amritsar
tradition says they heard it in the dry country to the south, where hunted Sikhs had taken refuge.
they rode in to seize treasure
the tradition sees no loot in it: they rode in to give the Harmandir back to its purpose.

games.q: you're Mehtab Singh, safe in the desert. news comes that the Harmandir is being used for drinking and dancing. you can't bring an army. what do you do?
o: stay safe and pray it ends.
ride in disguise, as men paying revenue, and end it yourselves.
write a complaint to the governor.
games.why: tradition says he and Sukha Singh rode in disguised as headmen with bags of false coins, struck down Massa Ranghar, and escaped.

practice: Bring to mind one thing that is sacred to you, or simply precious: a place, a practice, a person's dignity, a quiet hour you protect.

Notice where it's being crowded or mocked, even a little, even by your own habits, and let one small, peaceful way of giving it back its purpose come to mind. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Mehtab Singh. One of the two Sikhs who, with Sukha Singh, tradition says, rode into Amritsar in disguise to end Massa Ranghar's desecration of the Harmandir.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Harmandir Sahib, the house of the Guru at Amritsar.

carryVoice: Your line: they rode in. Not for loot, but for a holy place and what it stands for. A week, done.
